title: Compositional Basics in Landscape Photography: Dynamic Range, Transitions, and Minimal Post-Processing (AP PNW Part 5)

locations.name: Crater Lake, Oregon (Wizard Island)
locations.basis: Transcript references to Crater Lake and Wizard Island; discussion of framing and depth around Wizard Island

locations.name: Alaska (King Peak)
locations.basis: Explicit statement: 'clouds frame King Peak up in Alaska' (evidence of subject location)

locations.name: New Zealand
locations.basis: Transcript mentions 'helicopter to New Zealand' on last year's tour; used as location context for a layered composition

summary: This video articulates core compositional concepts for landscape photography through a painterly lens, emphasizing how the eye and camera perceive differently, how to manage dynamic range and exposure, and how to create depth and flow in a single frame. The instructor stresses dominant transitions (dark-to-light, cool-to-warm, big-to-small) to guide the viewer’s eye, advocates for careful spacing (edge control, rule of six) and the deliberate use of leading lines and layered structures, and discusses practical field techniques (wide-angle distortion, timing around sunrise, and the graph of light). In post-processing, the speaker outlines a minimalist workflow—prioritizing color grading and RAW adjustments, with occasional layer-based depth adjustments—and notes practical workflow considerations and occasional software instability. The transcript also grounds these ideas in real-world field examples, including references to Crater Lake (Wizard Island), Alaska, and New Zealand, and contrasts two- vs. three-dimensional perception in dynamic landscapes.

sections.title: Two-dimensional medium: eye vs camera
sections.description: Introduces the central premise that photography is a two-dimensional medium and highlights the need to understand how the eye sees differently than the camera, which frames the foundation for later compositional guidance.

sections.title: Dynamic range and exposure reality
concepts: Dynamic range in a single file
sections.description: Explains that dynamic range can be managed within a single exposure if highlights are controlled; shadows can be pulled with care, and histograms are not the sole guide. Mentions scenarios where merging exposures is unnecessary unless conditions push ISO high or highlights dominate.

sections.title: Motion, depth, and transitions in composition
concepts: Use of transitions to guide eye movement
sections.description: Discusses how perception changes with movement, why depth is hard to convey in a still frame with lots of detail, and introduces the concept of transitions (dark-to-light, large-to-small, etc.) to steer the viewer through the scene.

sections.title: Dominant transitions and layering
concepts: Level of blacks as depth cue
Layer separation in Photoshop for depth
sections.description: Outlines how to arrange subject matter with dominant transitions toward the light source and demonstrates layering as a means to create depth, including an example of separating layers with haze (post-process) to enhance perception of depth.

sections.title: Processing philosophy and Photoshop workflow
sections.description: Contrasts a minimalist processing philosophy (limited tools, emphasis on RAW adjustments and color grading) with explicit demonstrations of layer-based depth in Photoshop, followed by a stated preference against many common Photoshop features in the speaker’s workflow, highlighting the philosophy that technique should serve the image, not the toolkit.

sections.title: Graph of light and wide-angle rules
concepts: Graph of light concept and pre/post-sunlight glow
Wide-angle specific rules and peripheral distortion
Maximizing leading lines with camera placement
sections.description: Describes how light changes before and after sunrise/sunset and how to leverage that glow. Presents a dedicated wide-angle rule: position the camera to maximize distortion in the foreground to enhance leading lines and a big-to-small depth cue.

sections.title: Operational workflow and practical field tips
sections.description: Covers compositional discipline (rule of six, edge control, light source placement) and practical field constraints, including a workflow for evaluating frames and the importance of purposeful camera placement to maximize leading lines and transitions. Also notes a Photoshop crash and the need to save work with an open session.

sections.title: Wrap-up and ongoing work
sections.description: Wraps up the session with housekeeping: acknowledging software instability, and signaling that processing content continues in a follow-up step or later segment.

featured_techniques.technique: Single-exposure dynamic range management (avoid multi-exposure blending) when highlights are controlled
Level of Blacks as a depth cue; layering to create depth (in-field discussion and later Photoshop layering)
Dominant transitions (dark-to-light, cool-to-warm, big-to-small) to guide eye through frame
Rule of Six for composition; evaluate frame in six equal parts to prune clutter
Wide-angle leading lines via calibrated camera height to maximize peripheral distortion
Graph of light: pre/post-sun glow and its effect on exposure planning
Three kinds of light in photography (within-frame, side, back) and look-into-light guideline
Post-processing philosophy: color grading and RAW adjustments with a minimal toolset; avoidance of complex layering
Open step for non-destructive editing as a workflow practice
